## Overview

The Timucua were a Native American people who lived in Northeast and North Central Florida and southeast Georgia. Their territory extended from the Altamaha River and Cumberland Island south to Lake George, and from the Atlantic Ocean west to the Aucilla River. At European contact, Timucuan speakers occupied about 19,200 square miles and numbered an estimated 200,000 people. They were organized into as many as 35 chiefdoms rather than a single political unit. The Timucua spoke several dialects of Timucua, a language isolate, including Mocama, Potano, Itafi, Yufera, Agua Fresca, Acuera, and Oconi. Their folk-culture significance is documented through village organization, agriculture, hunting, tattooing, ball games, ceremonial drinks, mission-era records, and the surviving linguistic works of Francisco Pareja.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

Timucua clothing was made from moss and cloth created from various animal skins. The sources do not distinguish named garments, footwear, belts, or ceremonial clothing. Timucuan men wore their hair in a bun on top of their heads, which contributed to European observers’ impression of their height. The people were extensively tattooed, and tattoos were acquired through deeds and increasing responsibility. Children began to acquire tattoos as they took on more responsibility, while people of higher social class had more elaborate decorations. The tattoos were made by poking holes in the skin and rubbing ashes into them.

### Architecture

Timucua villages were commonly located near waterways. At the time of first European contact, villages of the Saturiwa and Agua Dulce typically contained about 30 houses and 200 to 300 people. Houses were small and circular, made from upright poles, and covered with palm-leaf thatching. A hole at the top provided ventilation and allowed smoke to escape. Houses were 15 to 20 feet across and were used primarily for sleeping.

Villages also had a council house, sometimes large enough to hold all the villagers; Europeans described some council houses as large enough for 3,000 people. When a village became too large, some families established another village nearby, forming clusters of related settlements. Each village or cluster had its own chief. Ceremonial mounds could stand in or near a village, although the mounds belonged to clans rather than villages.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They do describe agricultural tools, including the hoe and two sticks called *coa*, which women used to plant seeds. Crops were stored in granaries to protect them from vermin and the elements. Corn was ground into flour and made into corn fritters. The sources also mention bows and arrows in connection with archery.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The principal documented form of Timucua body adornment is tattooing. Each person was extensively tattooed, and tattoos marked deeds and increasing responsibility. Children began receiving tattoos as they took on more responsibility, while members of higher social class had more elaborate decorations. The process involved poking holes in the skin and rubbing ashes into the holes.

## Music & performance

They do record several performance-related practices. A chief’s council met every morning to discuss the problems of the chiefdom and smoke, beginning with the White Drink ceremony. The sources also describe dancing as a popular pastime and report that the Timucua played two related ball games.

Western Timucua played the “Apalachee ball game,” in which two teams of around 40 or 50 players kicked a ball toward a goal post. Hitting the post was worth one point, while landing the ball in an eagle’s nest at the top of the post was worth two points; the first team to score eleven points won. The western game was less associated with religious significance, violence, and fraud than the Apalachee version. Eastern Timucua played a similar game in which balls were thrown rather than kicked.

The Timucua also consumed a highly caffeinated tea called “black drink,” or “white drink” because of its purifying effects. It was made from the leaves of the yaupon holly tree and was consumed only by males in good status with the tribe. The drink was integral to most Timucua rituals and hunts.

## Dance & theatre

They state that dancing was a popular pastime and that the Timucua held victory celebrations for three days and nights after a successful raid. No further description of the movements, participants, music, costumes, or ceremonial structure is provided.

## Festivals & rituals

They document several ritual and communal practices. A chief’s council met every morning, and the meeting began with the White Drink ceremony. The drink, also called “black drink,” was made from yaupon holly leaves and had a purifying function; those who consumed it often vomited immediately. It was integral to most Timucua rituals and hunts and was consumed only by males in good status with the tribe.

After a successful raid, a tribe celebrated its victory for three days and nights. The sources also describe ceremonies connected with the chief’s council, hunting, and ball games. Timucua villages could contain ceremonial mounds, which belonged to clans rather than villages.

## Foodways

The Timucua were semi-agricultural and ate foods native to North Central Florida. They planted maize, beans, squash, and other vegetables, and may have employed crop rotation. Fire was used to clear fields of weeds and brush, and the soil was prepared with tools such as the hoe. Women planted seeds with two sticks called *coa*. Tobacco was also cultivated. Crops were stored in granaries, and corn was ground into flour and used to make corn fritters.

Timucua men hunted game, including alligators and manatees, and possibly whales. They fished in streams and lakes and collected freshwater and marine shellfish. Women gathered wild fruits, palm berries, acorns, and nuts, and baked bread from the root *koonti*. Meat was boiled or cooked over an open fire called the *barbacoa*, the source of the word “barbecue.” Fish were filleted and dried or boiled, while broths were made from meat and nuts.

After Spanish missions were established between 1595 and 1620, European foods were introduced, including barley, cabbage, chickens, cucumbers, figs, garbanzo beans, garlic, European grapes, European greens, hazelnuts, lettuce, melons, oranges, peas, peaches, pigs, pomegranates, sugar cane, sweet potatoes, watermelons, and wheat. Native corn became a traded item and was exported to other Spanish colonies.

## Oral tradition & literature

They do record a surviving Timucua text and a substantial missionary documentation tradition. Francisco Pareja produced a grammar, a confessional, and several Spanish–Timucua catechisms between 1612 and 1628. Gregorio de Movilla wrote two catechisms in Timucua and Spanish in 1635, and a Spanish-translated Timucuan letter to the Spanish Crown is dated 1688.

The Timucua language article includes a sample from Pareja’s *Confessionario*, presenting an interview with Timucua speakers preparing for conversion. In the passage, a priest asks whether the singing of a crow or another bird, together with trembling in the body, is believed to signal that people are coming or that something important is about to happen.

## Language & religion

Timucua is a language isolate formerly spoken in northern and central Florida and southern Georgia. At the time of Spanish colonization, it was the primary language used in the area. The language had nine or ten dialects, with differences that appeared mainly to mark band or tribal boundaries. Named dialects include Timucua proper, Potano, Itafi, Yufera, Mocama, Agua Salada, Tucururu, Agua Fresca, Acuera, and Oconi. Scholars disagree about whether Agua Salada was an alternative name for Mocama or a separate dialect.

Timucua was written by Franciscan missionaries in the 17th century using Spanish orthography. Francisco Pareja developed a writing system during 31 years of work with the Timucua. The language was agglutinative and synthetic, with prefixes, suffixes, and enclitics. It had no grammatical gender distinction or grammatical case, and its word order was subject–object–verb.

The sources describe Spanish missionization beginning in the late 16th century and the integration of Timucua communities into the mission system. The language is now extinct; after Spain ceded Florida to Great Britain in 1763, the few remaining Timucua speakers left for Cuba with Spanish colonists and mission Indians.
